exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule

question.explanation:
Note that plugging in $x = 0$ gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

\begin{align*} \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac {x\cos x}{\ln(x+1)} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{[x\cos x]'}{[\ln(x+1)]'} \\[5pt] & =\lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac {\cos{x} - x\sin{x}}{\left(\dfrac{1}{x+1}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\cos 0 - 0 \cdot\sin 0}{\left(\dfrac1{0+1}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{1}\\[5pt] &= 1 \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Note that plugging in $x = -1$ gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

\begin{align*} \lim_{x \to -1} \dfrac{x\ln(x+2)}{x^2 + 3x + 2} & = \lim_{x \to -1} \dfrac{[x\ln(x+2)]'}{[x^2 + 3x + 2]'}\\[5pt] & =\lim_{x \to -1} \dfrac{\left(\ln(x+2) + \dfrac{x}{x+2}\right)}{2x+3}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(\ln(-1+2) + \dfrac {-1}{-1+2}\right)}{2(-1)+3} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\ln(1) - 1}{1}\\[5pt] &= -1 \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice

question.explanation:
If we plug in $x = 0$ we get the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit: \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1-\cos(4x)}{x\sin(2x)} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\left[1-\cos(4x)\right]'}{[x\sin(2x)]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{4\sin(4x)}{\sin(2x)+2x\cos(2x)} \end{align}

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{1-\cos(4x)}{x\sin(2x)} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{4\sin(4x)}{\sin(2x)+2x\cos(2x)} \\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\left[4\sin(4x) \right]'}{\left[\sin(2x)+2x\cos(2x)\right]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{16\cos(4x)}{2\cos(2x)+2\cos(2x)-4x\sin(2x)}\\[5pt] & = 4\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\cos(4x)}{\cos(2x)-x\sin(2x)}\\[5pt] & = 4\cdot \dfrac{1}{1-0}\\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{4}. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice

question.explanation:
If we plug in $x = 0$ we get the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit: \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{xe^{-x}-x+2x^2}{\sin^2{x}} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{[xe^{-x}-x+2x^2]'}{[\sin^2{x}]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{(1-x)e^{-x}-1+4x}{2\sin{x}\cos{x}}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{(1-x)e^{-x}-1+4x}{\sin{2x}} \end{align}

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

\begin{align} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{xe^{-x}-x+2x^2}{\sin^2{x}} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{(1-x)e^{-x}-1+4x}{\sin{2x}}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{[(1-x)e^{-x} - 1+4x]'}{[\sin{2x}]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{(x-2)e^{-x}+4}{2\cos{2x}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{(0-2)e^0+4}{2\cos{0}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{-2+4}{2}\\[5pt] & = 1. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice

question.explanation:
If we plug in $x = 3$ we get the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit: \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2-6x+9}{16\sqrt{x+1}-4x-20} & = \lim_{x \to 3} \frac{\left[x^2-6x+9\right]'}{[16\sqrt{x+1}-4x-20]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{2x-6}{\left(\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{x + 1}} - 4\right)}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{x-3}{4(x + 1)^{-1/2} - 2} \end{align}

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{x^2-6x+9}{16\sqrt{x+1}-4x-20} & = \lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{x-3}{4(x + 1)^{-1/2} - 2} \\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{\left[x-3 \right]'}{\left[4(x + 1)^{-1/2} - 2\right]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{1}{-2(x+1)^{-3/2}}\\[5pt] & = - \dfrac{1}{2}\lim_{x \to 3} (x+1)^{3/2}\\[5pt] & = - \dfrac{1}{2}(3+1)^{3/2}\\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 8\\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-4}. \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating an Indeterminate Limit of the Form Infinity Divided by Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule

question.explanation:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are $\displaystyle \lim_{x \to 0^+} \ln(\sin{x}) = -\infty$ and $\displaystyle \lim_{x \to 0^+} \csc{x} = \infty,$ respectively, so we have the case $\dfrac{-\infty}{\infty}.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

\begin{align} \require{cancel} \lim_{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{\ln(\sin{x})}{\csc{x}} & = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{\left[ \ln(\sin{x}) \right]'}{[\csc{x}]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{\cot{x}}{-\csc{x}\cot{x}}\\[5pt] & = -\lim_{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{\cancel{\cot{x}}}{\csc{x}\cancel{\cot{x}}}\\[5pt] & = -\lim_{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{1}{\csc{x}}\\[5pt] & = -\lim_{x \to 0^+} \sin{x}\\[5pt] & = 0. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating an Indeterminate Limit of the Form Infinity Divided by Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule

question.explanation:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are $\displaystyle \lim_{x \to (\pi/2)^-} \ln\!\bigl(\sec x\bigr) = \infty$ and $\displaystyle \lim_{x \to (\pi/2)^-} \ln\!\bigl(\cot x\bigr) = -\infty,$ respectively, so we have the case $\dfrac{\infty}{-\infty}.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

\begin{align} \lim_{x \to (\pi/2)^-} \dfrac{\ln\!\bigl(\sec x\bigr)}{\ln\!\bigl(\cot x\bigr)} & = \lim_{x \to (\pi/2)^-} \dfrac{\left[\ln\!\bigl(\sec x\bigr)\right]'}{\left[\ln\!\bigl(\cot x\bigr)\right]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to (\pi/2)^-} \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\sec x \tan x}{\sec x}\right)}{\left(-\dfrac{\csc^2 x}{\cot x}\right)}\\[5pt] & = -\lim_{x \to(\pi/2)^-} \dfrac{\tan x \cdot \cot x}{\csc^2 x}\\[5pt] & = -\lim_{x \to (\pi/2)^-} \dfrac{\tan x \cdot \dfrac{1}{\tan x}}{\dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x}}\\[5pt] & = -\lim_{x \to (\pi/2)^-} \sin^2 x\\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-1}. \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule

question.explanation:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\dfrac{\infty}{\infty},$ so applying L'Hopital's rule yields \begin{align} \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{x^3}{\ln^2 x} & = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{[x^3]'}{[\ln^2 x]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{3x^2}{\left(\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\right)} \\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{3x^3}{2\ln x} \end{align}

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{\infty}{\infty}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get \begin{align} \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{x^3}{\ln^2 x} & = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{[3x^3]'}{\left[2\ln x\right]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{9x^2}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{9x^3}{2}\\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\infty}. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule

question.explanation: In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\dfrac{\infty}{\infty},$ so applying L'Hopital's rule yields \begin{align} \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac {2x^3-6}{x^2-4} & = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{[2x^3-6]'}{[x^2 - 4]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac {6x^2}{2x}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to \infty} 3x\\[5pt] & = \infty. \end{align}
